exercise_group.instruction: Unless otherwise specified, assume that all matrices in these exercises are $$n \times n$$ ﻿. Determine which of the matrices in Exercises 1–10 are invertible. Use as few calculations as possible. Justify your answers.

problem.paragraph: $$\left[\right. 5 & 7 - 3 & - 6 \left]\right.$$
$$\left[\right. - 4 & 6 6 & - 9 \left]\right.$$

exercise_group.instruction: In Exercises 11–20, the matrices are all $$n \times n$$ Each part of the exercises is an implication of the form “If ‘statement $$1$$ ’, then ‘statement $$2$$ ’.” Mark an implication as True if the truth of “statement $$2$$ ” always follows whenever “statement $$1$$ ” happens to be true. An implication is False if there is an instance in which “statement $$2$$ ” is false but “statement $$1$$ ” is true. Justify each answer.

problem.paragraph: (T/F) If the equation $$A\textbf{x = 0}$$ has only the trivial solution, then $$A$$ is row equivalent to the $$n \times n$$ identity matrix.
(T/F) If there is an $$n \times n$$ matrix $$D$$ such that $$AD = I$$ , then there is also an $$n \times n$$ matrix $$C$$ such that $$CA = I$$ .﻿
(T/F) If the columns of $$A$$ span $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ , then the columns are linearly independent.
(T/F) If the columns of $$A$$ are linearly independent, then the columns of $$A$$ span $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ .﻿
(T/F) If $$A$$ is an $$n \times n$$ matrix, then the equation $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ has at least one solution for each $$\textbf{b}$$ in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ .﻿
(T/F) If the equation $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ has at least one solution for each $$\textbf{b}$$ in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{\mathbf{n}}$$ , then the solution is unique for each $$\textbf{b}$$ .﻿
(T/F) If the equation $$A\textbf{x = 0}$$ has a nontrivial solution, then $$A$$ has fewer than $$n$$ pivot positions.
(T/F) If the linear transformation $$\mathbf{x}\mapsto A\textbf{x}$$ maps $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ into $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{\mathbf{n}}$$ , then $$A$$ has $$n$$ pivot positions.
(T/F) If $$A^{T}$$ is not invertible, then $$A$$ is not invertible.

(T/F) If there is a $$\textbf{b}$$ in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ such that the equation $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ is inconsistent, then the transformation $$\textbf{x}\mapsto A\textbf{x}$$ is not one-to-one.

An $$m \times n$$ upper triangular matrix is one whose entries below the main diagonal are $$0 \text{’s}$$ (as in Exercise 8). When is a square upper triangular matrix invertible? Justify your answer.

An $$m \times n$$ lower triangular matrix is one whose entries above the main diagonal are $$0 \text{’s}$$ (as in Exercise 3). When is a square lower triangular matrix invertible? Justify your answer.
Can a square matrix with two identical columns be invertible? Why or why not?
Is it possible for a $$5 \times 5$$ matrix to be invertible when its columns do not span $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{5}$$ ? Why or why not?
If $$A$$ is invertible, then the columns of $$A^{- 1}$$ are linearly independent. Explain why.

If $$C$$ is $$6 \times 6$$ and the equation $$C\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{v}$$ is consistent for every $$\mathbf{v}$$ in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{6}$$ , is it possible that for some $$\mathbf{v}$$ , the equation $$C\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{v}$$ has more than one solution? Why or why not?
If the columns of a $$7 \times 7$$ matrix $$D$$ are linearly independent, what can you say about solutions of $$D\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$$ ? Why?
If $$n \times n$$ matrices $$E$$ and $$F$$ have the property that $$EF = I$$ , then $$E$$ and $$F$$ commute. Explain why.

If the equation $$G{{\textbf{x}} = {\textbf{y}}}$$ has more than one solution for some $$\mathbf{y}$$ in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ , can the columns of $$G$$ span $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ ? Why or why not?
If the equation $$H{{\textbf{x}} = {\textbf{c}}}$$ is inconsistent for some $$\mathbf{c}$$ in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ , what can you say about the equation $$H\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$$ ? Why?
If an $$n \times n$$ matrix $$K$$ cannot be row reduced to $$I_{n}$$ , what can you say about the columns of $$K$$ ? Why?
If $$L$$ is $$n \times n$$ and the equation $$L\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$$ has the trivial solution, do the columns of $$L$$ span $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ ? Why?
Verify the boxed statement preceding Example 1.
Explain why the columns of $$A^{2}$$ span $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ whenever the columns of $$A$$ are linearly independent.

Show that if $$AB$$ is invertible, so is $$A$$ . You cannot use Theorem 6(b), because you cannot assume that $$A$$ and $$B$$ are invertible. [Hint: There is a matrix $$W$$ such that $$ABW = I$$ . Why?]
Show that if $$AB$$ is invertible, so is $$B$$ .﻿

If $$A$$ is an $$n \times n$$ matrix and the equation $$A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$$ has more than one solution for some $$\textbf{b}$$ , then the transformation $$\textbf{x}\mapsto\textit{A}\textbf{x}$$ is not one-to-one. What else can you say about this transformation? Justify your answer.
If $$A$$ is an $$n \times n$$ matrix and the transformation $$\textbf{x}\mapsto A\textbf{x}$$ is one-to-one, what else can you say about this transformation? Justify your answer.

Suppose $$A$$ is an $$n \times n$$ matrix with the property that the equation $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ has at least one solution for each $$\mathbf{b}$$ in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ . Without using Theorems 5 or 8, explain why each equation $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ has in fact exactly one solution.

Suppose $$A$$ is an $$n \times n$$ matrix with the property that the equation $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$$ has only the trivial solution. Without using the Invertible Matrix Theorem, explain directly why the equation $$A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$$ must have a solution for each $$\mathbf{b}$$ in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ .﻿

exercise_group.instruction: In Exercises 41 and 42, $$T$$ is a linear transformation from $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{2}$$ into $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{2}$$ ﻿. Show that $$T$$ is invertible and find a formula for $$T^{- 1}$$ ﻿.

problem.paragraph: $$T \left(\right. x_{1} , x_{2} \left.\right) = \left(\right. - 5 x_{1} + 9 x_{2} , 4 x_{1} - 7 x_{2} \left.\right)$$
$$T \left(\right. x_{1} , x_{2} \left.\right) = \left(\right. 6 x_{1} - 8 x_{2} , - 5 x_{1} + 7 x_{2} \left.\right)$$

Let $$T:\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ be an invertible linear transformation. Explain why $$T$$ is both one-to-one and onto $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ . Use equations (1) and (2). Then give a second explanation using one or more theorems.

Let $$T$$ be a linear transformation that maps $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ onto $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ . Show that $$T^{- 1}$$ exists and maps $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ onto $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ . Is $$T^{- 1}$$ also one-to-one?

Suppose $$T$$ and $$U$$ are linear transformations from $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ to $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ such that $$T(U{\textbf{x}) = \textbf{x}}$$ for all $$\mathbf{x}$$ in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ . Is it true that $$U\left( T{\left. \textbf{x} \right) = \textbf{x}} \right.$$ for all $$\mathbf{x}$$ in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ ? Why or why not?

Suppose a linear transformation $$T:\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{\mathbf{n}}\rightarrow\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{\mathbf{n}}$$ has the property that $$T(\textbf{u}) = T(\textbf{v})$$ for some pair of distinct vectors $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ . Can $$T$$ map $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ onto $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ ? Why or why not?

Let $$T:\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{\mathbf{n}}\rightarrow\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{\mathbf{n}}$$ be an invertible linear transformation, and let $$S$$ and $$U$$ be functions from $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ into $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ such that $$S\left( {T\left( \textbf{x} \right)} \right) = \textbf{x}$$ and $$U\left( {T\left( \textbf{x} \right)} \right) = \textbf{x}$$ for all $$\mathbf{x}$$ in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ . Show that $$U(\textbf{v}) = S(\textbf{v})$$ for all $$\mathbf{v}$$ in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ . This will show that $$T$$ has a unique inverse, as asserted in Theorem 9. [Hint: Given any $$\mathbf{v}$$ in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ , we can write $$\textbf{v} = T(\textbf{x})$$ for some $$\mathbf{x}$$ . Why? Compute $$S(\textbf{v})$$ and $$U(\textbf{v})$$ .]

Suppose $$T$$ and $$S$$ satisfy the invertibility equations (1) and (2), where $$T$$ is a linear transformation. Show directly that $$S$$ is a linear transformation. [Hint: Given $$\mathbf{u}$$ , $$\mathbf{v}$$ in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{\mathbf{n}},$$ let $$\textbf{x} = \textit{S}\left( \textbf{u} \right)$$ , $$\textbf{y} = \textit{S}\textbf{(v)}$$ . Then $$T\left( \textbf{x} \right) = \textbf{u}$$ , $$T\left( \textbf{y} \right) = \textbf{v}$$ . Why? Apply $$S$$ to both sides of the equation $$T\left( \textbf{x} \right) + T\left( \textbf{y} \right) = T\left( \textbf{x} + \textbf{y} \right)$$ . Also, consider $$T(c\textbf{x}) = cT({\textbf{x})}$$ .]

exercise_group.instruction: Exercises 50–52 show how to use the condition number of a matrix $$A$$ to estimate the accuracy of a computed solution of $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ ﻿. If the entries of $$A$$ and $$\mathbf{b}$$ are accurate to about $$r$$ significant digits and if the condition number of $$A$$ is approximately $$10^{k}$$ (with $$k$$ a positive integer), then the computed solution of $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ should usually be accurate to at least $$r - k$$ significant digits.

problem.paragraph: [T] Find the condition number of the matrix $$A$$ in Exercise 9. Construct a random vector $$\textbf{x}$$ in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{4}$$ and compute $$\textbf{b} = A\textbf{x}$$ . Then use your matrix program to compute the solution $$\textbf{x}_{1}$$ of $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ . To how many digits do $$\textbf{x}$$ and $$\textbf{x}_{1}$$ agree? Find out the number of digits your matrix program stores accurately, and report how many digits of accuracy are lost when $$\textbf{x}_{1}$$ is used in place of the exact solution $$\textbf{x}$$ .﻿
[T] Repeat Exercise 50 for the matrix in Exercise 10.

[T] Solve an equation $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ for a suitable $$\mathbf{b}$$ to find the last column of the inverse of the fifth-order Hilbert matrix $$A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 / 2 & 1 / 3 & 1 / 4 & 1 / 5 \\ 1 / 2 & 1 / 3 & 1 / 4 & 1 / 5 & 1 / 6 \\ 1 / 3 & 1 / 4 & 1 / 5 & 1 / 6 & 1 / 7 \\ 1 / 4 & 1 / 5 & 1 / 6 & 1 / 7 & 1 / 8 \\ 1 / 5 & 1 / 6 & 1 / 7 & 1 / 8 & 1 / 9 \end{bmatrix}$$

How many digits in each entry of $$\mathbf{x}$$ do you expect to be correct? Explain. [Note: The exact solution is $$\left( 630 \right.$$ , $$- 12600$$ , $$56700$$ , $$- 88200$$ , $$\left. 44100 \right)$$ .]

[T] Some matrix programs, such as MATLAB, have a command to create Hilbert matrices of various sizes. If possible, use an inverse command to compute the inverse of a twelfth-order or larger Hilbert matrix, $$A$$ . Compute $$AA^{- 1}$$ . Report what you find.
The columns of $$A$$ are obviously linearly dependent because columns $$2$$ and $$3$$ are multiples of column $$1$$ . Hence, $$A$$ cannot be invertible (by the Invertible Matrix Theorem).
If statement (g) is not true, then the equation $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ is inconsistent for at least one $$\textbf{b}$$ in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ .﻿

Apply the Invertible Matrix Theorem to the matrix $$A B$$ in place of $$A$$ . Then statement (d) becomes: $$A B\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$$ has only the trivial solution. This is not true. So $$A B$$ is not invertible.
